prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We have a friend in common, the retired sophomore. His concern: that I shall get it like that, in the right and righter of a green bush chomping on future considerations. In the ghostly dreams of others it appears I am all right, and even going on tomorrow there is much to be said on all these matters, “issues,” like “No rest for the weary.” (And yet—why not?) Feeling under orders is a way of showing up, but stepping on Earth—she’s not going to. Ten shades of pleasing himself brings us to tomorrow evening and will be back for more. I disagree with you completely but couldn’t be prouder and fonder of you. So drink up. Feel good for two. I do it in a lot of places. Subfusc El Dorado is only one that I know something about. Others are recently lost cities where we used to live—they keep the names we knew, sometimes. I do it in a lot of places. Brash brats offer laughing advice, as though anything I cared about could be difficult or complicated now. That’s the rub. Gusts of up to forty-five miles an hour will be dropping in later on tonight. No reason not to. So point at the luck we know about. Living is a meatloaf sandwich. I had a good time up there.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: His, And, Feeling

outputs.L1:
We have a friend in common: the retired sophomore. His concern is that I will receive it in just that way—in the right, and ever righter, manner of a green bush chewing over future considerations. In the ghostly dreams of others, I appear to be all right; and even tomorrow, there will still be much to say about all these matters—these “issues,” like “No rest for the weary.” And yet, why not?

Feeling under orders is one way of showing up, but as for stepping on Earth—she is not going to. Ten shades of pleasing himself bring us to tomorrow evening, and he will be back for more. I disagree with you completely, but I could not be prouder of you, nor fonder. So drink up. Feel good for two.

I do it in many places. Subfusc El Dorado is only one of them that I know something about. The others are recently lost cities where we used to live; sometimes, they keep the names we knew. I do it in many places.

Brash brats offer laughing advice, as though anything I cared about could now be difficult or complicated. That is the rub. Gusts of up to forty-five miles per hour will be dropping in later tonight. There is no reason they should not. So point toward the luck we know about. Living is a meatloaf sandwich. I had a good time up there.
outputs.L2:
We share an acquaintance: the former sophomore, now retired. What worries him is that I might receive it in just that manner—more and more correctly, as though from a green shrub chewing over what is still to come. In other people’s spectral imaginings, I seem to be doing fine; and even when tomorrow arrives, there will still be plenty to say about all of these things, these “issues,” such as “the tired never get relief.” (Still—why shouldn’t they?)

To act as if one is under command is one form of appearing, but as for setting foot on the Earth—she will not do that. Ten variations of self-satisfaction carry us forward to tomorrow night, and then there will be another return for more. I am in total disagreement with you, yet I could not feel more pride in you or more affection for you. So finish your drink. Feel well enough for two people.

I do this in many different locations. The dim, formal El Dorado is merely one place about which I know anything. The others are cities recently vanished, places where we once lived; sometimes they still preserve the names familiar to us. I do this in many different locations. Bold, unruly children give cheerful counsel, as if anything that mattered to me could still be hard or tangled now. That is the difficulty.

Later tonight, wind bursts reaching as high as forty-five miles per hour are expected to arrive. There is no particular reason they should not. So indicate the fortune we are aware of. Being alive is like a meatloaf sandwich. I enjoyed myself there.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on a shared acquaintance, allowing that memory to open into broader and more uncertain thoughts about the future. There is a sense of concern, though it remains somewhat vague, as if the speaker cannot quite name what is coming but feels its weight nonetheless.

Throughout the passage, there is a tension between obligation and endurance. The speaker seems burdened by responsibilities, expectations, or emotional ties, yet there is also a determination to keep going. Even when the future appears unclear or heavy, the movement forward continues.

At one point, the speaker expresses strong disagreement with another person, making it clear that they do not share that person’s view or decision. However, this disagreement does not cancel out affection. On the contrary, the speaker also reveals pride, warmth, and admiration, suggesting a relationship complicated by both conflict and love.

The past is presented through images of places that feel like lost cities. These remembered locations may no longer exist in the same way, or may have changed beyond recognition, yet some of them still carry familiar names. This creates a feeling of nostalgia, as if memory preserves fragments of a vanished world.

There is also a sense of luck, as though the speaker recognizes how much depends on chance. Finally, the speaker expresses gratitude for the experience itself, appreciating that, despite uncertainty, difficulty, and loss, there was still a good time to be had.
outputs.L4:
Uncertainty is not an interruption of life, but one of its most reliable conditions. It arrives before breakfast, sits beside the bed, follows us into the street, and waits patiently in the pauses between one thought and another. Some mornings it looks like a letter we are afraid to open. Some nights it looks like the face of someone we loved and did not understand in time. It asks questions in a voice that sounds almost like our own: What if you chose badly? What if you have forgotten something essential? What if everyone else has been given instructions and you alone are improvising?

Memory does not answer these questions clearly. Memory is no orderly archive, no clean room full of labeled drawers. It is more like a house after a storm: a photograph under the sofa, a cup on the windowsill, a song coming from a room that may not exist anymore. We remember a hand on our shoulder, but not the day. We remember the weather, but not the apology. We remember being certain, which is perhaps the strangest memory of all. Certainty feels, in retrospect, like a coat we once wore as children and somehow believed would fit forever.

And then there is affection, stubborn and unreasonable. It survives embarrassment, distance, bad timing, and all the little failures by which people injure one another without meaning to. Affection is there in the ridiculous advice we give to those we cannot protect: eat something warm, take an umbrella, do not trust a man who speaks too softly about investments, never buy pears when you are sad. We offer these instructions as if they were charms against catastrophe. We cannot prevent loss, illness, misunderstanding, or the long bureaucratic machinery of disappointment, so we say, “Wear good shoes,” and hope the universe will take the hint.

At times the mind, overwhelmed by its own seriousness, begins to speak in dreams. A fish appears in the hallway carrying a briefcase. A grandmother who has been dead for twenty years scolds the moon for wasting electricity. The ceiling lowers itself politely, as if not wishing to alarm anyone. A parade of officials marches through the kitchen to announce that all citizens must now be happy by Thursday. In such moments, reality reveals how thin its uniform is. Beneath the daily schedule, beneath bills and appointments and the necessary lies we tell to keep ourselves functional, there is a wild, comic disorder. We are all trying to behave normally on a planet that spins in darkness.

Perhaps this is why disagreement can feel both tragic and absurd. We argue over politics, money, memory, tone of voice, the correct version of events, the meaning of a silence at dinner. Each person carries a private weather system and insists it is the climate. One says, “You never listened,” and the other says, “I listened all my life.” Both may be right. Both may be wrong. More likely, both are standing in the ruins of what they meant to say, pointing at different walls.

Still, even amid confusion, life keeps producing its small invitations. The kettle boils. A dog sleeps with complete philosophical confidence in a patch of sun. Someone laughs in the next room, not politely but helplessly, and for a moment the whole heavy structure of existence becomes lighter. There is bread to toast, a shirt to mend, a message to answer, a plant that has not given up despite neglect. These things are not solutions. They do not erase grief or repair the past. But they are evidence. They suggest that continuing is not always a grand moral decision; sometimes it is simply the next ordinary act.

We live under pressures that often seem absurd: to be successful but not vain, kind but not weak, informed but not despairing, productive but not exhausted, sincere but not inconvenient. We are expected to know who we are, explain where we are going, and improve ourselves continuously, even while the floorboards of the world creak beneath us. It is no wonder that the inner voice becomes fragmented, that it skips from childhood to prophecy to grocery lists to imagined conversations with the dead. The mind is not broken because it wanders. It wanders because it is trying to make a map of fog.

And maybe the map does not need to be perfect. Maybe it is enough to mark a few places honestly: here I was afraid; here I was loved; here I made a mistake; here I laughed when I thought I could not; here I continued. The road ahead may be difficult. There may be more losses, more arguments, more mornings when the news sounds like a threat and the heart feels like an object misplaced in a crowded station. But there will also be the ridiculous persistence of pleasure: soup on a cold evening, clean sheets, a familiar voice, the first green insistence of spring, the private comedy of being human and not quite equal to the task.

To continue, then, is not to understand everything. It is not to become fearless, untouched, or wise in any permanent way. It is to move through uncertainty with one hand extended, feeling for walls, for furniture, for another hand. It is to accept that memory will distort, affection will ache, advice will fail, and dreams will interrupt the proceedings. It is to admit that life is fragmented and often impossible to summarize, yet still full of moments that gleam. Confusion remains. Difficulty remains. But so does humor. So does tenderness. So does the strange, ordinary courage of waking up again and seeing what can be made of the day.
outputs.L5: His hands trembled slightly as he opened the old letter. And in that quiet moment, he realized how much the past still lived inside him. The feeling was not sadness exactly, but something softer—a mix of memory, hope, and gratitude. He smiled, folded the letter carefully, and placed it back where it belonged, knowing that some emotions never truly fade.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the style of John Ashbery, with drifting logic, odd idioms, weather-report intrusions, and a tone that mixes affection, disagreement, and nostalgia.
counterfactuals.output:
The afternoon had been folded wrong,  
creased along the river where the ducks were practicing  
their small disputes with eternity. I was saying,  
yes, I remember, but not like that—  
not with the blue chair wearing your hat  
and the window making weather at us.

A low-pressure system is moving in from the west,  
bringing scattered apologies by evening,  
with a chance of clarinets in the outlying districts.

You laughed, which was unnecessary  
and therefore dear. The cupboard stood open  
like a minor official who has forgotten his errand.  
Inside: three spoons, a postcard from Tuesday,  
and the old argument, still fresh as parsley,  
about whether happiness is a room  
or merely the rumor of someone leaving one.

I meant to agree with you completely,  
but the floor had other ideas. It sloped toward childhood,  
where the lawns were damp and enormous  
and everyone called supper by a different name.  
There were bicycles asleep in the rain.  
There was your hand, or a hand I have promoted  
to yours after years of paperwork.

Visibility reduced to one mile in fog;  
drivers are advised to use memory sparingly.

Of course we were wrong. That was our specialty.  
We kept putting the moon in practical places—  
the glove box, the sugar bowl, under the dog—  
and then complaining that the night lacked management.  
Still, I miss the way you contradicted the lamps,  
how you could make a whole house lean forward  
just by refusing to answer.

Now the map grows little whiskers.  
The town has moved again, politely,  
leaving behind its bandstand and several opinions.  
I walk there sometimes in my sleep  
and buy a newspaper full of yesterday’s snow.  
The headline says: YOU WERE KIND, BUT INCORRECT.  
I fold it under my arm like a wounded swan.

Tomorrow will be partly cloudy,  
except where the past persists,  
in which case residents may experience  
brief intervals of golden dust and mild regret.

Listen—if that is still the verb.  
I have saved the buttons from your blue coat,  
though not the coat, though not the winter,  
though not the exact expression  
with which you forgave me nothing  
and almost everything. The garden, meanwhile,  
continues its green exaggeration.  
Each rose insists it was present at the beginning.  
Each weed votes no.

And I, who loved you in the old sideways manner,  
with pockets full of string and weather,  
am still standing here beside the misdelivered morning,  
arguing softly with your absence  
because it knows the way home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a paragraph of dreamlike, semi-coherent literary prose that sounds like an experimental mid-century American poem, including phrases like “No rest for the weary,” “I disagree with you completely,” and “Living is a meatloaf sandwich.”
counterfactuals.output: At the blue hour the streetlights opened like tired lilies, and the newspaper boys were already old men whispering, “No rest for the weary,” into the sleeves of their raincoats; above them the moon dragged its tin spoon through the soup of heaven, stirring up lost addresses, trumpet notes, a tooth, a map of Kansas folded into a sparrow. I met you there beside the pharmacy of sleep, your pockets full of thunder and nickels, and when you said the river was only a hallway pretending to move, I said, “I disagree with you completely,” though my mouth was full of feathers and yesterday’s ash. The city kept breathing in square windows, the dogs debated eternity under parked cars, and somewhere a mother ironed the ocean flat. “Living is a meatloaf sandwich,” announced the blind clock from the courthouse tower, and everyone nodded, chewing the warm, strange bread of morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an avant-garde monologue from an unreliable narrator, full of non sequiturs, strange metaphors, repeated lines, and references to lost cities, wind gusts, friendship, and future considerations.
counterfactuals.output:
I was not there when the city sank, although I remember the taste of its streetlamps.

That is the first thing you must understand.

The second thing is this: wind has opinions. It arrives at the window with its pockets full of broken glass and says, *Consider the future.* As if the future were a small animal I had forgotten to feed. As if I had not already laid out a plate for it, silver fork, blue napkin, a chair facing the wall.

I was not there when the city sank.

But I held the rope.

Or perhaps the rope held me.

There are lost cities everywhere if you know how to misread a map. Atlantis under the tongue. El Dorado in the glove compartment. Ys ringing its drowned bells beneath the mattress where I kept your letters, your teeth, your promises of friendship written in green ink and weather. We were friends, weren’t we? Say yes. Say it into this tin can. Say it before the gust comes back and translates us into birds.

The wind gusts were strongest on Tuesdays.

No, that is impossible. There were no Tuesdays then. Only brass afternoons and one long hallway with a piano at the end. The piano was full of bees, naturally. Every civilized instrument is. I played it once and the whole room apologized.

Friendship is a table with one leg shorter than the others. You sit anyway. You eat the soup anyway. You pretend the wobbling is music.

I was not there when the city sank.

I was the city.

You see the problem.

My doctor says memory is a house with too many doors. My butcher says doors are only knives with manners. My mother says nothing because she is a photograph of a staircase, and every night I climb her until I reach the attic of my own mouth. Up there: dust, pigeons, a calendar from the year after the world ends.

Future considerations must be filed in triplicate.

One copy for the sea.

One copy for the wind.

One copy for the friend who never arrives but whose coat remains on the chair, breathing.

Do not ask me what happened to the city. Cities are always losing themselves. One minute they are avenues, bakeries, women leaning from balconies to shake crumbs into the dawn; the next they are coral, rumor, a museum exhibit titled *Possible Water*. I tried to warn them. I stood in the square and shouted, “The clocks are filling with rain!” But everyone thought I was selling onions.

Perhaps I was selling onions.

Perhaps I made a fortune.

Listen: the gust comes sideways when it means yes. It comes from below when it means no. It comes carrying feathers when it wants to be forgiven. Last winter a wind gust entered my room and knocked over the vase you gave me, the one shaped like a lighthouse, the one we stole from that hotel in Carthage, or Cleveland, or some other empire with excellent towels.

The vase did not break.

It simply forgot its shape.

Like you.

Like me.

Like the city I was not there to lose.

We were friends, weren’t we? I need this confirmed for the record. The record is a black lake spinning at the center of the room. The needle descends. The needle says: *Again.*

We were friends, weren’t we?

We were friends, weren’t we?

We were—

No. Wait. I remember now. You were a bridge. I was the toll. People passed through us carrying baskets of figs and prophecies, and none of them paid. This is why civilization collapses: insufficient exact change.

Lost cities have excellent acoustics. In Pompeii, the ash repeats your name until it becomes a recipe. In Tikal, the jungle wears temples like old crowns. In the ruins of Mohenjo-daro, the drains still dream of rain. And beneath all of them, under every brick and bone, there is a little clerk stamping papers: *Future consideration denied. Future consideration pending. Future consideration misplaced in a gust of wind.*

I admire bureaucracy. It is the only art form that can drown standing up.

I was not there when the city sank.

I was busy teaching a mirror how to lie.

It was a gifted pupil.

By morning it told me I looked innocent.

By noon it told me the sea had no motive.

By evening it wore my face better than I did and left for the capital with a suitcase full of thunder.

If you see it, do not trust it. If you see me, do not trust that either.

The truth is a staircase made of eels. The truth is a hat full of wet matches. The truth is that I held your hand when the sirens began, unless I didn’t, unless your hand was a lantern, unless the sirens were gulls, unless the entire emergency was merely a rehearsal for a play about furniture.

Still, I recall the wind.

A gust like a door slamming in God’s ribs.

A gust like horses made of flour.

A gust like an old friend turning away before you can say, “Stay, there are future considerations.”

Future considerations.

What a phrase. It walks into the room wearing my father’s shoes. It taps the floor with a cane made of tomorrow’s bones. It asks whether I have prepared a statement. I have. It is written on the inside of my eyelids in the ink of lost harbors:

I was not there when the city sank.

I was not there when the city sank.

I was not there when the city sank.

And yet every night I wake with seaweed in my pockets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a found-poetry style passage that feels like fragments from letters, weather forecasts, casual conversation, and philosophical musings stitched together into one absurd but emotionally resonant text.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear whoever is still checking the mailbox,

A warm front is moving in from the west  
carrying pollen, low visibility, and several apologies  
that were not postmarked in time.

By evening, expect scattered sentences.  
Possible thunderstorms after midnight.  
Possible forgiveness by Thursday,  
though models disagree.

I saw your sister at the grocery store—  
no, not that sister, the one with the laugh like a drawer full of spoons—  
and she said, *Can you believe this weather?*  
which is what we say when we mean  
the world has continued without asking us first.

Please water the basil.  
Please don’t read the last paragraph.  
Please understand that when I said I was leaving  
I meant in the small, daily way,  
like steam leaving a cup,  
like birds revising the sky.

Meanwhile, the pressure is falling.

A man on the bus announced that time is only a rumor  
started by clocks to sell more ticking.  
Everyone looked at their phones.  
The baby in the blue hat applauded.  
I wanted to tell you this immediately  
but all my messages were drafted in rain.

There is a 60% chance of finding your old sweater  
behind the chair where grief keeps its library.  
There is a 90% chance I will smell cedar  
and become unreasonable.

Listen—  
the moon was out at noon today, pale as a receipt,  
and nobody panicked.  
Perhaps that is maturity:  
seeing an impossible thing  
and continuing to buy onions.

You once wrote,  
*I don’t know how to be happy without making a project of it.*  
I folded that line into a paper boat  
and it sank in the kitchen sink  
beside a spoon, a lemon seed,  
and one bright unanswerable question.

Roads may be slick in low-lying areas.  
Travel is not advised  
unless you are returning to someone  
or finally leaving.

“Do you want the rest of my fries?”  
“Yes.”  
“Are you okay?”  
“Yes.”  
The tiny lies of civilization,  
passed hand to hand like salt.

In conclusion,  
no conclusion has been issued.  
The horizon remains under review.  
The heart, that amateur meteorologist,  
keeps pointing at the dark clouds and saying,  
*This too is weather. This too will move.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intentionally nonsensical yet poetic piece about a shared friend, feeling under orders, pride and fondness, and remembering places that may no longer exist, ending with “I had a good time up there.”
counterfactuals.output:
Our mutual friend wore a weather vane for a hat  
and insisted the north wind owed him three apologies.  
We believed him, of course, because belief was on the schedule,  
and all morning the orders came down like silver spoons:  
stand here, salute the wallpaper, admire the invisible horse.

I was proud of him in the way a lighthouse is proud of fog—  
confused, glowing, and entirely involved.  
Fond, too, though fondness had become a small blue engine  
running backward through my ribs,  
whistling whenever he laughed.

Do you remember the stairway behind the bakery,  
the one that led to the moon or possibly the laundry room?  
Do you remember the field where the statues practiced breathing,  
the hotel with no doors,  
the town square that folded itself into a paper crane  
and flew off before breakfast?

Maybe none of it is there now.  
Maybe none of it was ever there.  
Still, I keep its map in my coat pocket,  
drawn in jam, annotated by birds,  
creased where your name and his name meet.

We were under orders, yes—  
from the trumpet, from the rain,  
from whatever captain lives inside old affection.  
But pride stood beside us, polishing its buttons,  
and fondness kept handing out warm oranges in the dark.

If you see our friend, tell him the clouds have forgiven him.  
Tell him the north wind is still writing.  
Tell him I remember every impossible room.

I had a good time up there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
